uruk.name: Uruk
uruk.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian city that, at its peak around 3100 BC, may have been the largest urban settlement in the world, with tens of thousands of residents.

jemdet-nasr.name: Jemdet Nasr
jemdet-nasr.summary: A Sumerian settlement mound in Iraq's Babil Governorate, giving its name to the Jemdet Nasr period (c. 3100–2900 BC); excavations there uncovered early proto-cuneiform tablets.

akkad-city.name: Akkad
akkad-city.summary: Capital of the Akkadian Empire, the dominant political power in Mesopotamia for about 150 years in the late 3rd millennium BC; its exact location remains unknown.

isin.name: Isin
isin.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian city in what is now Iraq, occupied from the late 4th millennium BC to at least the late 1st millennium BC, whose patron deity was the healing goddess Gula.

larsa.name: Larsa
larsa.summary: An ancient Sumerian city-state near Uruk in what is now Iraq, center of the sun god Utu's cult and a source of Babylonian mathematical tablets.

abisare.name: Abisare
abisare.summary: Amorite ruler of the ancient city-state of Larsa who died around 1895 BC; records from his 11-year reign describe him striking the city of Isin in his 9th regnal year.

neo-assyrian-empire.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
neo-assyrian-empire.summary: An ancient Mesopotamian empire beginning in 911 BCE that grew to dominate the Near East, Egypt and parts of Anatolia, described as history's first world empire.

burney-relief.name: Burney Relief
burney-relief.summary: A Mesopotamian terracotta relief from about 1800 to 1750 BCE showing a winged, nude goddess-like figure flanked by owls and standing on lions; now in the British Museum.

inanna.name: Inanna (Ishtar)
inanna.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian goddess of war, love and sex, originally worshipped in Sumer and later known as Ishtar among the Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians.

lion-of-babylon-statue.name: Lion of Babylon
lion-of-babylon-statue.summary: A stone sculpture over 2,600 years old found in Babylon, Iraq, once attributed to Nebuchadnezzar II but now thought by most experts to be Hittite.

stele-of-the-vultures.name: Stele of the Vultures
stele-of-the-vultures.summary: A monument from 2600–2350 BC Mesopotamia celebrating Lagash's king Eannatum defeating the rival city of Umma; the earliest known war monument, mostly held today in the Louvre.

eannatum.name: Eannatum
eannatum.summary: A Sumerian ruler of Lagash around 2450 BC who built one of the first verifiable empires, subduing Elam, destroying Susa, and dominating Sumer and Akkad.

lagash.name: Lagash
lagash.summary: An ancient Sumerian city-state near the Euphrates and Tigris rivers in what is now Iraq, one of the oldest cities of the ancient Near East.

umma.name: Umma
umma.summary: Ancient Sumerian city in what is now Iraq, likely the leading city of the Early Dynastic kingdom of Gišša, whose tutelary gods were Sara and Ninura.

gilgamesh.name: Gilgamesh
gilgamesh.summary: Hero of Mesopotamian mythology and protagonist of the Epic of Gilgamesh, possibly a real king of Uruk around 2900–2350 BCE who was later worshipped as a god.

humbaba.name: Humbaba
humbaba.summary: A giant-like guardian of the cedar forest in Mesopotamian mythology, killed by the hero Gilgamesh and his companion Enkidu, an act that angered the gods.

cedar-forest.name: Cedar Forest
cedar-forest.summary: The realm of the gods in Mesopotamian mythology, guarded by the demigod Humbaba, where the hero Gilgamesh cut down cedar trees in the Epic of Gilgamesh.

sargon-of-akkad.name: Sargon of Akkad
sargon-of-akkad.summary: First ruler of the Akkadian Empire, who conquered Sumeria's city-states in the 24th to 23rd centuries BC and is sometimes seen as history's first emperor; he later became a legendary figure in Assyrian literature.

akkadian-empire.name: Akkadian Empire
akkadian-empire.summary: An ancient kingdom established around 2300 BCE, often considered the first empire in world history, uniting Akkadian and Sumerian speakers across Mesopotamia under Sargon of Akkad and his successors.

early-dynastic-period-mesopotamia.name: Early Dynastic Period (Mesopotamia)
early-dynastic-period-mesopotamia.summary: An era in Mesopotamia, roughly 2900 to 2350 BC, marked by competing city-states before Sargon united the region as the Akkadian Empire.

late-bronze-age-collapse.name: Late Bronze Age collapse
late-bronze-age-collapse.summary: A sudden societal collapse across the Eastern Mediterranean and Near East in the late 13th to early 12th century BC, ending major Bronze Age powers like the Hittite Empire.

sea-peoples.name: Sea Peoples
sea-peoples.summary: A group of tribes who raided Egypt and other eastern Mediterranean regions around 1200 BC, once seen as a main cause of the Bronze Age collapse but now often viewed as refugees fleeing an ongoing crisis.

hittites.name: Hittites
hittites.summary: An Anatolian Indo-European people who built one of the first major Bronze Age civilizations in West Asia, forming an empire centered on the capital Hattusa that peaked in the mid-14th century BC under Šuppiluliuma I before collapsing by the 12th century BC.

mari-syria.name: Mari
mari-syria.summary: An ancient Semitic city-state on the Euphrates in modern Syria that flourished as a trade hub linking Sumer and the Levant from about 2900 to 1759 BCE.

subartu.name: Subartu
subartu.summary: A Bronze Age kingdom or region in Upper Mesopotamia, whose exact location is uncertain, later used by the Akkadian Empire as a term meaning "north".

elam.name: Elam
elam.summary: An ancient civilization centered in western and southwestern Iran, one of the leading political forces of the ancient Near East, with written records from around 3000 BCE.

gutians.name: Gutians
gutians.summary: An ancient Near Eastern people whose conflict with the Akkadian Empire is linked to its collapse; they later ruled southern Mesopotamia as the Gutian dynasty of Sumer.

zagros-mountains.name: Zagros Mountains
zagros-mountains.summary: A 1,600 km mountain range spanning Iran, northern Iraq, and southeastern Turkey, running from Iran's western border to the Persian Gulf.

sumer.name: Sumer
sumer.summary: The earliest known civilization, in southern Mesopotamia (now south-central Iraq), emerging between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE; its cities produced the world's earliest known written texts.

third-dynasty-of-ur.name: Third Dynasty of Ur
third-dynasty-of-ur.summary: A Mesopotamian dynasty based in Ur in the 21st century BCE, briefly the region's dominant power; founded by Ur-Namma and expanded into an empire by his son Shulgi before collapsing around 2004 BCE.

hammurabi.name: Hammurabi
hammurabi.summary: Sixth Amorite king of Babylon (r. c. 1792-1750 BC) who unified much of Mesopotamia and issued a famous law code emphasizing punishment of offenders.

old-assyrian-period.name: Old Assyrian period
old-assyrian-period.summary: The early stage of Assyrian history centered on the city of Assur, from about 2025 to 1363 BCE, when its rulers were governors rather than kings and Assur became a hub of international trade.

ramesses-ii.name: Ramesses II
ramesses-ii.summary: Third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty (c. 1303–1213 BC), often called Ramesses the Great; his 66-year reign, the longest of any pharaoh, included 15 military campaigns.

shasu.name: Shasu
shasu.summary: Semitic-speaking pastoral nomads of the Southern Levant from the late Bronze Age into the Iron Age, organized in clans under tribal chieftains and sometimes serving as mercenaries.

moab.name: Moab
moab.summary: An ancient kingdom in what is now southern Jordan, along the Dead Sea, known from the Mesha Stele and often in conflict with its Israelite neighbors.

battle-of-kadesh.name: Battle of Kadesh
battle-of-kadesh.summary: A major c.1274 BCE battle between Ramesses II of Egypt and Muwatalli II of the Hittites, the earliest pitched battle in recorded history with known tactics, ending in stalemate.

lugal-zage-si.name: Lugal-zage-si
lugal-zage-si.summary: King of Umma who briefly united Sumer as a single kingdom and was the last Sumerian king before Sargon of Akkad's conquest around 2334 BC.

enshakushanna.name: Enshakushanna
enshakushanna.summary: King of Uruk around the mid-3rd millennium BC, named on the Sumerian King List, who conquered Hamazi, Akkad, Kish and Nippur to claim hegemony over Sumer.

kish-sumer.name: Kish
kish-sumer.summary: An important archaeological site in Iraq near ancient Babylon, occupied from the Ubaid period to the Hellenistic period, whose patron deities included Ishtar and later Zababa.

horemheb.name: Horemheb
horemheb.summary: Last pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty, ruling from about 1319 to 1292 BC, who rose from army commander to restabilize the country after the Amarna Period.

apiru.name: ʿApiru
apiru.summary: A term used in 2nd-millennium BCE Near Eastern texts for outlaws, mercenaries, raiders and laborers of low social status; once wrongly linked directly to the word "Hebrew."

merneptah.name: Merneptah
merneptah.summary: Fourth pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, reigning for almost ten years from 1213 BC; son of Ramesses II, best known for the stele mentioning Israel.

battle-of-megiddo-15th-century-bc.name: Battle of Megiddo
battle-of-megiddo-15th-century-bc.summary: A 15th-century BC battle in which Pharaoh Thutmose III's Egyptian forces defeated a Canaanite coalition led by the king of Kadesh, the earliest battle recorded in reliable detail.

thutmose-iii.name: Thutmose III
thutmose-iii.summary: Pharaoh of Egypt's 18th Dynasty who ruled from 1479 to 1425 BCE, led 17 to 20 victorious military campaigns, and created Egypt's first navy, earning him the nickname "the Napoleon of Egypt."

cuneiform.name: Cuneiform
cuneiform.summary: The earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay, developed for Sumerian and later adapted for Akkadian and other ancient Near Eastern languages.

ebla.name: Ebla
ebla.summary: One of the earliest kingdoms in Syria, a trading empire that flourished in the 3rd millennium BCE whose discovery proved the Levant rivaled Egypt and Mesopotamia as an ancient center of civilization; destroyed by the Hittites around 1600 BC.

ur.name: Ur
ur.summary: A major Sumerian city-state in ancient Mesopotamia dating from about 3800 BC, whose patron deity was the moon god Nanna and whose ziggurat still stands partially restored.

shuruppak.name: Shuruppak
shuruppak.summary: Ancient Sumerian city (modern Tell Fara) on the Euphrates in Iraq, south of Nippur, dedicated to Ninlil, the goddess of grain and air.

abu-salabikh.name: Abu Salabikh
abu-salabikh.summary: Archaeological site of a small Sumerian city near ancient Nippur in Iraq, occupied from the Neolithic through the late third millennium BCE, with ties to Kish, Mari and Ebla.

amorites.name: Amorites
amorites.summary: A Northwest Semitic-speaking Bronze Age people from western Mesopotamia who ruled much of the Levant and Mesopotamia from about the 21st to 16th century BC, founding Babylon.

kassites.name: Kassites
kassites.summary: A people from the Zagros Mountains who controlled Babylonia under the Kassite dynasty from about 1531 to 1155 BC, ruling first from Babylon and later from Dur-Kurigalzu.

enmebaragesi.name: Enmebaragesi
enmebaragesi.summary: Penultimate king of the first dynasty of Kish, around 2750 BC, the earliest ruler on the Sumerian King List confirmed directly by archaeological evidence.

sexagesimal.name: Sexagesimal
sexagesimal.summary: A base-60 number system invented by the ancient Sumerians and passed on to the Babylonians, still used today in modified form for time and angles.

eponym-dating-system.name: Eponym dating system
eponym-dating-system.summary: A calendar system used in Assyria for over a thousand years, in which each year was named for an official called the limmu, lasting until the Assyrian Empire's end in the 7th century BC.

uruk-period.name: Uruk period
uruk-period.summary: The era, roughly 4000 to 3100 BC, when the first cities and states arose in Mesopotamia, named after the city of Uruk where innovations like the potter's wheel appeared.

ancient-egyptian-calendar.name: Egyptian calendar
ancient-egyptian-calendar.summary: A 365-day solar civil calendar used in ancient Egypt, split into three 120-day seasons plus five extra days, which slowly drifted out of step with the true solar year.

dendrochronology.name: Dendrochronology
dendrochronology.summary: The scientific method of dating tree rings to the exact year they formed, useful for precise dating too recent for radiocarbon methods and for calibrating them.

chronology-of-the-ancient-near-east.name: Floating chronology
chronology-of-the-ancient-near-east.summary: A dating framework for the ancient Near East that lacks firm absolute dates, used for periods like early Bronze Age Mesopotamia where dendrochronology and reliable radiocarbon sequences are missing.
chronology-of-the-ancient-near-east.source_title: Chronology of the ancient Near East

harappa.name: Harappa
harappa.summary: Ancient city in Punjab, Pakistan, that gave its name to the Indus Valley Civilisation's Mature Harappan phase (2600–1900 BC), with up to 23,500 residents at its height.

nippur.name: Nippur
nippur.summary: An ancient Sumerian city in what is now Iraq, the special seat of worship of the god Enlil, occupied from the Ubaid period onward.

kassite-dynasty.name: Kassite dynasty
kassite-dynasty.summary: The line of Kassite-origin kings who ruled Babylon from 1595 to 1155 BC, the longest dynasty of that state, preserving Babylonian traditions while restoring order and expanding culture.

middle-assyrian-empire.name: Middle Assyrian Empire
middle-assyrian-empire.summary: Assyria's first period as an empire, from about 1363 BC to 912 BC, during which it became the dominant power of northern Mesopotamia.

new-kingdom-of-egypt.name: New Kingdom of Egypt
new-kingdom-of-egypt.summary: The period of ancient Egypt from about the 16th to 11th century BC, covering the 18th to 20th dynasties, marking Egypt's greatest power and territorial extent.

naram-sin-of-akkad.name: Naram-Sin
naram-sin-of-akkad.summary: A ruler of Akkad who reigned around 2255–2218 BC, grandson of Sargon, under whom the empire reached its greatest extent and who was the first Mesopotamian king to claim divinity.

king-of-the-four-corners.name: King of the Four Corners
king-of-the-four-corners.summary: A title of ancient Mesopotamian rulers claiming dominion over the whole known world, first used by Naram-Sin in the 23rd century BC and later revived by Assyrian and Persian kings.

ashur-uballit-i.name: Ashur-uballit I
ashur-uballit-i.summary: King of Assyria from about 1363 to 1328 BC, whose defeat of the Mitanni marked Assyria's rise as a powerful empire and led to early Assyrian intervention in Babylonian affairs.

mitanni.name: Mitanni
mitanni.summary: A Hurrian-speaking kingdom in northern Syria and southeast Anatolia, around 1550 to 1260 BCE, a major regional power bordered by the Hittites, Egyptians, Kassites and Assyrians.

tukulti-ninurta-i.name: Tukulti-Ninurta I
tukulti-ninurta-i.summary: King of Assyria who reigned around 1243 to 1207 BC and was the first ruler known to use the title 'King of Kings.'

ka-tilia-u-iv.name: Kaštiliašu IV
ka-tilia-u-iv.summary: The 28th Kassite king of Babylon, ruling around 1232 to 1225 BC, whose war against Assyria ended in a catastrophic defeat.

tukulti-ninurta-epic.name: Epic of Tukulti-Ninurta
tukulti-ninurta-epic.summary: An Assyrian epic in Akkadian glorifying King Tukulti-Ninurta I's wars against Babylon's King Kashtiliash IV, seen as a form of royal propaganda.

kara-hardash.name: Kara-hardash
kara-hardash.summary: A king of Babylon with an Assyrian mother who took the throne around 1333 BC but was killed shortly after in an anti-Assyrian revolt, prompting his grandfather to invade in response.

kurigalzu-ii.name: Kurigalzu II
kurigalzu-ii.summary: 22nd king of the Kassite dynasty of Babylon (c. 1332–1308 BC), placed on the throne by the Assyrian king Aššur-Uballiṭ I; he reigned 25 years before turning on his former allies.

dilmun.name: Dilmun
dilmun.summary: Ancient civilization in eastern Arabia covering modern Bahrain, Kuwait and eastern Saudi Arabia, a major Bronze Age trading centre between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley described in Sumerian myth as a paradise.

kidin-hutran.name: Kidin-Hutran
kidin-hutran.summary: A Middle Elamite king of the Igihalkid dynasty known for wars against Babylonia, including raids that deposed Babylonian kings.

ugarit.name: Ugarit
ugarit.summary: An ancient Levantine coastal city in what is now northern Syria, also known as Ras Shamra; excavations since 1928 revealed the oldest known systematic use of an alphabet.

bay-chancellor.name: Bay
bay-chancellor.summary: An Asiatic-born official who rose to power in ancient Egypt under Seti II and became a key power broker in the late 19th Dynasty, until his death in 1192 BC.

ammurapi.name: Ammurapi
ammurapi.summary: Last Bronze Age king of the Syrian city of Ugarit, reigning around 1215 to 1180 BC and a contemporary of the last Hittite king, Suppiluliuma II.

uppiluliuma-ii.name: Šuppiluliuma II
uppiluliuma-ii.summary: Last known great king of the Hittite New Kingdom, reigning about 1207 to 1178 BC; his fleet defeated the Cypriots in what is recorded as history's first naval battle.

el-deity.name: El
el-deity.summary: A Northwest Semitic word for 'god', and the name of the supreme deity of ancient Canaanite religion, described as father of the gods and creator of humanity.

asherah.name: Asherah
asherah.summary: A major goddess in ancient Semitic religions, associated with fertility, motherhood and sacred trees, worshipped as consort to the god El or, in some accounts, Yahweh.

baal.name: Baal
baal.summary: A Northwest Semitic title meaning 'lord', applied to gods and especially associated with the storm and fertility god Hadad, worshipped across the Levant, Egypt and the Mediterranean.

anat.name: Anat
anat.summary: A goddess of warfare and hunting best known from the Ugaritic texts, portrayed in myths such as the Baal Cycle as a staunch ally of the weather god Baal.

dagon.name: Dagon
dagon.summary: A god worshipped across ancient Syria and Mesopotamia, seen as father of the gods, lord of the land and source of royal legitimacy; the Hebrew Bible names him the Philistines' national god.

sin-mythology.name: Sin (Nanna)
sin-mythology.summary: Mesopotamian god of the moon, also called Nanna, associated with cattle herding, the crescent symbol, and sometimes seen as a judge of the dead.

giorgio-buccellati.name: Giorgio Buccellati
giorgio-buccellati.summary: Italian archaeologist best known for discovering the ancient Hurrian capital of Urkesh (modern Tell Mozan) in Syria.

ashur-god.name: Ashur (god)
ashur-god.summary: The national god of the Assyrians in ancient times, worshipped until their gradual conversion to Christianity between the 1st and 5th centuries AD.

assur.name: Assur
assur.summary: An ancient city on the Tigris River, capital of the Middle and Neo-Assyrian Empires, occupied for roughly 3,000 years until sacked in the mid-3rd century CE.

marduk.name: Marduk
marduk.summary: The patron god of Babylon, worshipped as a god of creation, justice and magic, who rose to become leader of the Mesopotamian pantheon by the 2nd millennium BC.

ugaritic-texts.name: Ugaritic texts
ugaritic-texts.summary: A corpus of about 1,500 cuneiform texts found at Ugarit, written in the 13th and 12th centuries BCE in the otherwise unknown Ugaritic language, including epic poems, myths, and records.

ebla-tablets.name: Ebla tablets
ebla-tablets.summary: A collection of up to 1,800 complete clay tablets and thousands of fragments from the palace archives of ancient Ebla in Syria, dating to about 2500 to 2250 BC and discovered in 1974 to 1975.

emar.name: Emar
emar.summary: A Bronze Age trade city at Tell Meskene in Syria, known from thousands of cuneiform tablets recording private legal and business transactions until its fall around 1187 BC.

elohim.name: Elohim
elohim.summary: A Hebrew word meaning 'gods' or 'godhood' that usually refers to a single deity, often the God of Judaism, despite its plural form, though it can also mean gods in the plural or judges.

hieros-gamos.name: Hieros gamos
hieros-gamos.summary: A sacred marriage ritual between gods, sometimes reenacted symbolically by human participants representing the deities, regarded as a prototype of fertility rituals.

akkadian-language.name: Akkadian language
akkadian-language.summary: The earliest documented Semitic language, spoken in ancient Mesopotamia from the mid-third millennium BC until gradually replaced by Aramaic by the 8th century BC, written in cuneiform script.

sumerian-language.name: Sumerian language
sumerian-language.summary: The language of ancient Sumer, attested from at least 3100 BCE and unrelated to any other known language; it survived as a sacred, ceremonial and scientific language until the 1st century CE even after Akkadian became everyday speech.

enlil.name: Enlil
enlil.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian god of wind, air, earth and storms, chief deity of the Sumerian pantheon, worshipped at the Ekur temple in Nippur from the 24th century BC.

ninhursag.name: Ninhursag
ninhursag.summary: Ancient Sumerian mother goddess of the mountains and one of the seven great deities of Sumer, known from myths describing her dealings with the god Enki.

ubaid-period.name: Ubaid period
ubaid-period.summary: A prehistoric period of Mesopotamia lasting roughly from 6500 to 3800 BC, marking the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian alluvial plain.
